lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Hey Rachel, can you hear me okay? I think my headset just decided to update itself thirty seconds before the call.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Yeah, I can hear you fine. Classic. Mine did that yesterday in front of our CFO, so you're in good company.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Ha, perfect. Well, thanks for making the time. I know it's a Friday and you're probably buried in end of month stuff.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: It's fine. Honestly this is the most interesting meeting on my calendar today, which says a lot about my calendar.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: I'll take it. So I've got us for thirty minutes. My goal is mostly to listen and understand what's going on at Acme, and then if it makes sense, we can talk about next steps. Does that work?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Works for me. I have a hard stop at eleven thirty though, I have a carrier review right after.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Got it, I'll keep an eye on the clock. So to start, you filled out the form on our site mentioning shipment delay analytics. Can you walk me through what's happening today?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Sure. So we move about eleven thousand shipments a week, mostly regional freight across the Midwest and the Southeast. And our on time rate dropped from ninety four percent to about eighty seven percent over the last two quarters.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Seven points is a lot. Do you know why yet?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: That's the problem, we kind of don't. We have theories. Some of it is carrier capacity, some of it is our warehouse in Memphis, which has been, let's say, a character building experience. But we can't slice the data fast enough to prove anything.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Okay. And where does that data live right now?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: It's all in Snowflake. Events from our TMS, scan events from the warehouses, and the carrier API feeds. Then we've got Looker on top of it, which is where the pain really starts.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Tell me about the Looker pain. I hear that a lot, but I want to hear your version.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: So every time an ops manager has a question, like, why were Tuesday shipments out of Memphis late, they file a ticket with our data team. And our data team is two people. The average turnaround is something like six business days.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Six days. So by the time the answer comes back, the problem's already--

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Already moved, yeah. Or it fixed itself, or it got worse. It's like getting a weather report for last week.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: That's a great way to put it. And what does that cost you, roughly? Like if you had to put a number on the late shipments.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: We actually did that exercise for the board. Late deliveries cost us about three hundred and forty thousand dollars last quarter in penalties and credits to customers. And that doesn't count the churn. We lost one account, Hartwell Foods, partly because of reliability.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Ouch. How big was Hartwell?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: About one point two million a year. So, you know, it stung. My CEO still brings it up in every staff meeting.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Yeah, I bet. Okay so if I'm hearing you right, the core need is: ops managers need to answer delay questions themselves, same day, without waiting on the data team. Is that fair?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: That's exactly it. And ideally get alerted before it becomes a problem. Like, if Memphis dwell time spikes on a Monday, I want to know Monday, not the following Friday.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Got it. So alerting on leading indicators, not just reporting on lagging ones.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Yes. You should put that on a slide.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Ha, it probably already is on one somewhere. Okay, so who would actually use this day to day? How many people are we talking about?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Core users, probably twelve ops managers, plus my two regional directors, plus me. Then maybe another thirty people who'd just look at dashboards, like account managers who want to show customers their on time numbers.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Okay, so roughly fifteen power users and thirty viewers. That's helpful. And the two people on the data team, would they be involved?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Oh, very. Tariq runs the data team, and honestly he's going to be the one who decides if the integration is real or if it's a toy. He's been burned before.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Burned how?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: We tried a tool two years ago, I won't say the name, but it basically required us to re-instrument everything and send events to their cloud. It took four months and we gave up. So Tariq's first question is going to be, do you sit on top of Snowflake or do we have to move data.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Good question, and I'll give you the short answer now. We connect directly to Snowflake with a read only role. No data movement required for the core dashboards. For real time alerting we can also ingest a stream, but that's optional.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Okay, that's, yeah, that's the right answer. He'll still want to see it.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Of course. I'd love to set up a technical session with Tariq and our solutions engineer. Is that something you could help arrange?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Yeah, I can do that. He's out next week at a conference, but the week after should be fine.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Great. Let's come back to that. Can I ask about budget? I don't want to waste your time if we're way off.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Sure, no, I appreciate you asking directly. We've set aside somewhere between sixty and eighty thousand a year for this. That's approved in principle by our CFO, Dan Whitley.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Okay. And is that new budget or is it replacing something?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Partly replacing. We pay about forty five thousand for Looker right now, and that contract ends January thirty first. If we find something better, Dan's happy to redirect that money plus some.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: That's really helpful. So there's a natural forcing date there, January thirty first.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Right. And honestly I'd rather not renew Looker for another full year just because we ran out of time. That's kind of my nightmare scenario.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Makes sense. So who ultimately signs off? Is it you, is it Dan, is there a committee?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: So I'm the one who owns the problem and I'll make the recommendation. Dan signs anything over fifty thousand. And Tariq basically has a veto on the technical side. He can't say yes alone, but he can definitely say no.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Ha, the classic technical veto. Okay. And is there anyone in procurement or legal we should know about?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Yeah, we have a procurement person, Janet, and a security questionnaire that is, I'm not kidding, a hundred and twelve questions. Last vendor took three weeks to get through it.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: We have a SOC 2 Type Two report and a pre filled answer set for most of the standard questionnaires, so hopefully we can beat three weeks. Could you send me the questionnaire early so we can start in parallel?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Yeah, that's smart. I'll ask Janet to send it over. Probably Monday.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Perfect. And what does the paper process look like after security? Like, redlines, MSA, that kind of thing?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: We usually want to use our own MSA. Legal takes about two weeks for redlines. Then Dan signs. So if you add it up, from a verbal yes to a signature, call it five weeks.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Okay, so working backwards from January thirty first, you'd want a decision by around mid December.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: I'd actually like to decide by end of Q4, so December nineteenth at the latest. Everyone disappears after that for the holidays.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Understood. December nineteenth. I'll write that down in big letters. Are you looking at anyone else right now?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Yeah, I'll be honest. We're talking to Amplitude and we're also looking at just hiring a third data analyst and staying on Looker.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: That's fair, and I appreciate the honesty. What do you like about the Amplitude option so far?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: They're well known, the board has heard of them. But the demo felt very web product focused, like funnels and signups. We don't have signups, we have trucks.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Ha, yeah, trucks don't sign up very often. And the analyst option, what's the thinking there?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: It's roughly the same money, maybe a hundred and ten thousand fully loaded. But it doesn't fix the core problem, which is that questions go into a queue. It just makes the queue a bit shorter.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Right. It scales the bottleneck instead of removing it.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Exactly. That's the argument I'm going to make to Dan, so feel free to help me make it.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Happy to. Actually, that brings up something I wanted to ask. What would success look like for you in, say, six months? If we did this and it went well.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Honestly? On time rate back above ninety two percent. And the ops managers never filing a ticket for a delay question again. If I could show Dan a number like that, penalties down by half, that pays for this ten times over.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: That's a really clear success metric. Ninety two percent on time, penalties cut in half. I'd love to build the business case around those.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Please do. I'm terrible at business cases. I just want the trucks to be on time.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: That's what we're here for. Quick question about the data itself. Do your scan events have a consistent shipment ID across the TMS and the warehouse systems?

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Mostly. Memphis uses a different WMS that was, uh, inherited from an acquisition, and their IDs have a prefix. Tariq has a mapping table for it.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Okay, that's very normal. We can handle that with a join in the model. I'll flag it for our SE so it's in the technical session.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Good. That's exactly the kind of thing that killed the last project.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Noted. So let me try to summarize and you tell me what I got wrong.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Go for it.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: On time rate dropped from ninety four to eighty seven percent. Late deliveries cost about three hundred forty thousand last quarter, plus you lost Hartwell. Ops managers wait six days for answers from a two person data team. You need self serve analysis and proactive alerting on top of Snowflake.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Yep. So far so good.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Budget is sixty to eighty thousand, approved in principle by Dan Whitley. You make the recommendation, Dan signs, Tariq has a technical veto, Janet runs procurement. Looker ends January thirty first, and you want a decision by December nineteenth. You're also looking at Amplitude and at hiring an analyst.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: That's, yeah, that's scarily accurate. Did you record this?

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Ha, I did, with your permission at the start. It's how I don't forget anything.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Right, right. Okay. So what are next steps from your side?

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Three things. First, I'll send you a recap email today with everything we just said, so you can forward it to Dan and Tariq. Second, I'll set up a technical deep dive with Tariq and our SE, Arjun, for the week after next, once he is back. And third, once Janet sends the security questionnaire, we'll turn it around within five business days.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: That sounds great. Can we also do a demo with some of our actual data? Like a sandbox? The ops managers won't believe it unless it's their own shipments.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We do a two week proof of value. If Tariq can give us a read only role on a sample schema, we can have Memphis dwell time dashboards and alerts running in a couple of days.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Okay, I love that. Let's aim for that right after the technical session.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Deal. And one more ask. Would you be open to being the internal champion for this? Mostly it means helping me understand what Dan needs to see to say yes.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Yeah, I'm already the champion, I just didn't have the title. Dan is going to want payback period, and he's going to want a reference customer in logistics.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: We have a couple. Coastline Freight is probably the closest match, similar size. I'll ask their VP of ops if she'd take a twenty minute call with you.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: That would help a lot. Dan trusts peers more than vendors. No offense.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: None taken, I wouldn't trust me either. Alright, I'll have the recap to you by end of day, the reference intro by Wednesday, and I'll send calendar options for the technical session.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Perfect. And I'll get Janet to send the questionnaire Monday and I'll talk to Tariq about the read only role.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Awesome. Thanks Rachel, this was genuinely one of the clearest discovery calls I've had in a while.

lines.speaker: rachel
lines.text: Thanks Ethan. Go fix your headset.

lines.speaker: ethan
lines.text: Ha, it's first on my list. Have a good carrier review.
